date_basis: RIB: archaeological context (late 1st c.); attribution to the Ninth is probable, not certain
rank: [... l]eg(ionis) VIII[I] - soldier/officer of the Ninth (rank lost)
rib_commentary:
1.  The name is a cognomen in -ianus formed from a simpler cognomen (e.g. Scaeva) or a nomen (e.g. Naevius). Unless it is unique, there are very few possibilities. The only one that occurs
 more than once or twice is Naevianus.
 2.  The suprascript bar extends to the very edge of the fragment, confirming the trace
 of a third vertical stroke in the numeral, and implying that a fourth has been lost.
 Either [L]EG VIII or [L]EG VIII [I] could be read, but in a first-century British context the Ninth Legion is almost certain; there is no evidence that the Eighth contributed to the invasion-force (Keppie 1971). Compare RIB 3047 for another early altar from southern Britain which may have named the Ninth.
 It is unclear whether RIB 3042 identified the legion by its cognomen, but probably not, since it is omitted by its
 four earliest tombstones in Britain (RIB 254, 255, 256 and 257; the fifth from Lincoln, RIB 260, is broken here). It is also apparently omitted by RIB 3047.

find_context: Found re-used in Holy Trinity church, Godmanstone (SY 666 974), 7 km north of Dorchester, from where it probably came; but the church is only 1.5 km north of the Roman villa at Forston
text: Perhaps I(ovi) O(ptimo) [M(aximo)] Tit[us ..] pini[us (centurio)] l[eg(ionis)] V[ΙΙII] v(otum) s(olvit) [l(ibens) m(erito)]
text_diplomatic: Perhaps I O [.] TIT[...] PINI[...] ❦ L[..] V[...] V S [..]
translation: To Jupiter Best and Greatest, Titus [..]pinius centurion of the [Ninth] Legion paid his vow willingly, deservedly.
date_basis: RIB: "very early", military occupation of Dorset (no explicit date); numeral restored
rank: (centurio) l[eg(ionis)] V[IIII] - centurion of the [Ninth] Legion (restored)
rib_commentary:
2–3.  Examination of the stone does not support Wright’s reading of E. To find room for the centurial sign, he conjectured a short and unattested cognomen,
 Pine[s], a variant of the unique Pannonian name Pinnes (Velleius ii, 110, 4), but this is improbable. If we must read a nomen and cognomen, only Tit[ius Pa]|pini[anus] or Al]|pini[anus] seem possible, but they leave no room for the centurial sign. But since the altar
 apparently belongs to the military occupation of Dorset, and is thus very early, the dedicator conceivably did not have a cognomen; the likeliest
 nomen is Papinius, but Alpinius (from the cognomen Alpinus) is also possible. See further below.
 4–5.  The leaf-stop (hedera) is only explicable if it was balanced by another to the right, to fill the space
 either side of L[EG] and its numeral/cognomen, and to emphasise them. (For this decorative function, but
 a century later, compare RIB 3014 and 3115.) Wright thought the reading was ‘probably L[EG XX] | V [V]’, but this would be lop-sided and leave the leaf-stop unexplained. The reading L[EG] | V[I V] would be possible, but the legion did not arrive in Britain until fifty years after the army left Dorset. So the reading L[EG] | V[IIII] is required. The omission of the cognomen is not difficult: it is also omitted by
 the legion’s earliest tombstones in Britain (RIB 254, 255, 256, 257; 260 is uncertain), three of which incidentally attest legionaries who have no cognomen
 either. The presence of a centurion of the Ninth in Dorchester(?) is difficult to explain, but this problem is also posed by RIB 3042.

RIB restores L[EG] V[IIII]: Wright's L[EG XX] V[V] would be lop-sided; L[EG] V[I V] impossible because Legio VI arrived fifty years after the army left Dorset; so "the reading L[EG] | V[IIII] is required", cognomen omitted as on the earliest Lincoln tombstones. This form of L, with sloping foot, occurs occasionally on dies of the Sixth Legion (RIB 2460.61 and 79), and on one of the Twentieth Legion (2463.11); it is also found on stamps of Legion VIII Augusta at Strasbourg (R. Forrer, Strasbourg-Argentorate i (1927), Taf. III.52, IV.65, V. 78), but these are in no other way comparable with the Leicester stamp.
 Haverfield (loc. cit.) interpreted the stamp as l(egio) (octava), ‘The Eighth Legion’. Keppie, however, has shown (loc. cit.) that there is no evidence for the presence of Legion VIII in Britain in a.d. 43, which would in any case be too early a context for the stamping of legionary tiles
 in Britain. A vexillation of Legion VIII was in Britain during the reign of Hadrian (see RIB 2426.1), but it is unlikely that a vexillation on active service would be making tiles;
 and why one of its products should appear at Leicester cannot be convincingly explained. At Strasbourg the Legion’s number on tile-stamps is invariably followed by AVG, A, or some other title.
 The absence of a stop following L has led to a suggestion that the stamp represents a numeral (‘58’); yet this is hard to explain on a die (batch-numbers usually taking the form of
 graffiti) and, as Davies Pryce (loc. cit.) observed, a stop is also absent in this position on stamps of Legion V Alaudae at Xanten.
 Although at first sight the die appears complete, Professor E. Birley in 1955 suggested (in litt. to R.P.W.) that the stamp was from a broken die of >Legion VIIII, and that the apparent straight edge at the left hand end of the impression was created
 by fracture along the final digit.
 It will be noticed that the die has no surrounding margin, such as would have strengthened
 it against breakage. Even without a margin, however, a fracture at the final digit,
 almost at the edge of the die, would be unexpected. But the proportions of the stamp
 are unusual, and they suggest that the original die contained more than the letters
 LVIIII. Comparison with RIB 2462.4, a stamp of the same height as the Leicester stamp and a length of 156 mm, raises the suspicion that RIB 2462.1 was once of similar length, which would be required by the restoration proposed in
 the text. The fracture would then have occurred in a more probable position, near
 the middle of the die. If this were of wood, and the digits carved out along the axis
 of the grain, a straight fracture could have occurred along the furrow of the numeral’s
 final I as the result of a sharp tap to clear the die of clay. Parts of the L in particular are shallow, as if the matrix was partly choked.

rib_commentary:
There is a slight bar over X.
 The Lincoln provenance is almost certainly erroneous. The object was acquired by the Lincoln Museum in 1910 from the sale of the Stamford Institution, and the Museum Register gives the provenance as Lincoln. But the Sale Catalogue lists only ‘Portions of Roman tiles from York’, and there is no record of stamped tiles having been found at Lincoln in c. 1850. Moreover, the object is made in a York fabric (information from Ian Betts).
 It is unlikely that tiles were stamped by the legion before its transfer to York in a.d. 71. See the Introduction, p. 125.

rib_commentary:
The tegula was almost certainly made at York. There is no evidence that tiles were stamped while the legion was at Lincoln.
 Stamped with the die of 2462.9 when the foot of the L and the suprascript bar had worn away or been choked with clay. On some 9A stamps

 or not at all. The impressions thus come late in the use of the die, after wear; but
 it is often impossible to make a firm distinction between 2462.9 and 9A, especially when the stamp is fragmentary.
